cues.text: Section six: cost optimisation and sourcing.
Cost optimisation seeks the best value from expenditure, while maintaining the required quality, security and resilience.
This is different from cost cutting, which merely reduces spending.
Consider an example: removing backup infrastructure may reduce today's bill, but it can increase tomorrow's losses.
Next, let us look at cost drivers.
These include compute, storage, networking, software licences, staffing, vendor contracts, integration, support and technical debt.
To understand where money goes, analyse cost by service, by department, by environment and by business unit.
Unit economics, such as cost per transaction or cost per delivery, connects expenditure to output, so that spending can be judged against what it produces.
Now to cloud FinOps.
Cloud FinOps brings engineering, finance and business teams together to manage variable cloud spending.

The techniques include tagging resources, allocating costs, budgeting, anomaly detection, rightsizing, scheduling idle environments, removing genuinely unused assets, applying storage lifecycle policies, and using appropriate committed-use discounts.
Two related ideas support accountability.
Showback reports consumption costs to departments, while chargeback allocates those costs to their budgets.
Both encourage accountability.
However, poor allocation rules can create disputes, or discourage the use of shared services.
Finally, sourcing.
Sourcing choices include in-house delivery, outsourcing, managed services, cloud services and hybrid arrangements.
Outsourcing can provide expertise and flexible capacity, but it creates dependency, as well as security, quality and contract risks.
When evaluating a sourcing option, consider total cost, service levels, intellectual property, data handling, exit options and vendor performance.
And remember: do not outsource accountability.
